segments.caption: Wellington. 128, off 153 balls. Rishabh Pant's ninth Test hundred.
But to understand Pant, forget the hundreds.
Watch what happens to a Test match when he walks in.
Since his debut, top-order batters in Test cricket have scored at 53 runs per 100 balls. Pant scores at 74.
With him at the crease, India score at almost four an over. Without him, just over three.
That speed is time.
At an ordinary pace, his runs would have taken more than 300 extra overs. That's three and a half days of Test cricket, handed back to India's bowlers.
And he plays like this when the match is slipping.
Sydney, 2021. India need 407. While his partners crawl, Pant makes 97 off 118, and Australia start to worry.
A week later at the Gabba, 89 not out wins the chase, and the series.
Ahmedabad. In at 80 for 4, out with a hundred. India win by an innings.
His other weapon is the six. 108 in Tests, second only to Ben Stokes. Almost one in five of India's Test sixes since 2018.
Most of them come off spin. Against spinners, he averages 53, at 86 runs per 100 balls.
Nathan Lyon got him out six times. Pant took 258 runs, and seven sixes, off him.
Then, on 30 December 2022, a car crash nearly ended everything.
637 days later, in his first Test back, he made a hundred at Chennai. India won.
At Leeds in 2025, a hundred in each innings. At Manchester, he batted on a fractured foot.
And he does it where it's hardest.
Away from home, no leading keeper of the last two decades averages more, has more hundreds, or scores faster.
The same instinct has a price. Seven times, he's fallen in the nineties, against nine hundreds.
Across Test cricket, fewer than one in five 90-plus scores stop short. For Pant, it's almost half.
So don't judge Rishabh Pant by his average. Judge him by the match.
When he walks in, the game starts moving. And rarely at the pace the opposition wants.
Beyond The Scoreboard.
